item.title: [Retailing 101 #11] Why One Corner Prints Money and the Next Block Over Goes Dark
item.body:
> Retail real estate isn't about finding a "good spot" — it's about matching a specific store format to the specific pool of people who can realistically reach it.

## Today's Concept

There's an old line in retail: the three things that matter are location, location, and location. It's a cliché, but it survives because store location is one of the few decisions you can't undo cheaply. You can re-merchandise a shelf on Tuesday. You can drop prices tonight. You cannot move a 30,000-square-foot building with a 15-year lease.

Location strategy breaks into three questions that get asked in order.

**1. What factors make a site work?** Retailers evaluate sites on a handful of measurable things:

- **Traffic** — vehicle counts (published by state DOTs as annual average daily traffic, or AADT) and foot traffic. But raw volume isn't enough. Cars doing 55 mph past a median-divided highway can't turn left into your parking lot.
- **Accessibility** — curb cuts, signal lights, left-turn access, parking ratio (commonly around 4–5 spaces per 1,000 sq ft for shopping centers), and how easy it is to get *out* as well as in.
- **Visibility** — sightlines from the road, signage rights, and how far ahead a driver can spot you.
- **Trade area demographics** — population, household income, age mix, and daytime population (the workers who show up 9-to-5 but sleep elsewhere).
- **Competition and co-tenancy** — nearby stores that steal your customers versus ones that deliver them. A nail salon wants to be next to a grocery anchor. A furniture store is happy next to another furniture store, because shoppers comparison-shop big-ticket items.
- **Cost and terms** — base rent per square foot per year, CAM (common area maintenance) charges, percentage rent, lease length, and any exclusivity or co-tenancy clauses.

**2. Who can actually reach it?** That's **trade area analysis**. A trade area is the geographic zone a store draws customers from, usually split into three rings:

- **Primary** — roughly 50–70% of customers, closest in
- **Secondary** — the next 20–30%
- **Tertiary** — the scattered remainder, including people passing through

Practitioners rarely draw simple circles anymore. They use **drive-time polygons** (a 5-, 10-, and 15-minute drive radius, which bends around rivers, highways, and dead ends) and, increasingly, anonymized mobile-location data showing where customers actually came from.

The classic analytical tool is the **gravity model**. The intuition is borrowed from physics: a store's pull grows with its size and shrinks with the distance (or travel time) shoppers must cover.

```
attraction ≈ store size ÷ (travel time)^k
```

The Huff model formalizes this — it estimates the *probability* a given household shops at Store A rather than Store B, which is more useful than a hard boundary line, because real trade areas are fuzzy and overlapping. A related check is **cannibalization**: if your new store's trade area overlaps an existing one you already own, part of your "new" sales is just sales moving across town.

**3. What kind of site is it?** Location types come with built-in trade-offs:

- **Unplanned / freestanding** — a standalone building, often a pad or outparcel at the edge of a shopping center lot. Cheap per square foot, great parking, full signage control, but no neighbor pulling traffic for you. Works for destination brands (Walgreens, a drive-thru quick-service restaurant).
- **Central business district (CBD)** — downtown. High daytime population, high rent, limited parking, weekend traffic that can fall off a cliff in office-heavy districts.
- **Strip / neighborhood center** — a line of stores with surface parking, usually anchored by a supermarket or a drugstore. Built for convenience and errand trips.
- **Power center** — a cluster of big-box category killers (home improvement, pet supply, off-price apparel). Draws from a wide radius.
- **Enclosed regional mall** — big trade area, high traffic, high rent, strict operating rules and long leases.
- **Lifestyle center** — open-air, upscale, restaurant-heavy; sells atmosphere and dwell time.
- **Airports, campuses, transit hubs** — captive audiences, premium pricing, brutal rent and operating restrictions.

The right answer depends entirely on format. A convenience store needs a right-turn-in on the evening commute side of the road. A destination retailer like IKEA can sit by a highway interchange 25 minutes away and still fill the lot, because people plan the trip.

## In Everyday Life

Think about a Starbucks and a Costco in the same American suburb.

The Starbucks sits on the *morning* side of a busy arterial — the inbound-commute side — with a right-turn-in entrance and a drive-thru wrapping the building. Its primary trade area may be only a mile or two wide. Nobody plans a 20-minute drive for a latte, so it lives on interception: catching a trip already in progress. That's why you'll see two Starbucks locations facing each other across the same road. They're not competing so much as covering opposite commute directions, and the company accepts a bit of cannibalization to own both flows.

Costco plays the opposite game. There's one per region, usually near a freeway interchange with a huge lot and a gas station out front. People will drive 25 minutes and load a cart with $250 of goods. Its trade area is measured in a 15-minute-plus drive time, not blocks. The gravity model explains both: Costco's enormous size overcomes distance decay, while Starbucks' small size means it must live very close to its customer.

Now look at the strip mall nearby. The grocery anchor probably pays $8–$15 per square foot in annual base rent, while the small inline shops next to it might pay $30–$45, plus $5–$10 in CAM. The anchor pays less because it *generates* the traffic everyone else feeds on. And many small-shop leases include a **co-tenancy clause**: if the anchor goes dark, the small tenant can cut rent or walk. That clause exists precisely because their location value came from the neighbor, not the address.

## Three-Line Summary

1. Site selection weighs traffic, accessibility, visibility, trade-area demographics, competition and co-tenancy, and total occupancy cost — not just rent.
2. Trade area analysis defines who can realistically reach a store, using drive-time zones and gravity/Huff models that trade hard boundaries for probabilities, while watching for cannibalization of your own stores.
3. Location type — freestanding, CBD, strip center, power center, mall, lifestyle center, or captive venue — must match the store's format, because convenience retailers intercept trips while destination retailers can pull people across a whole metro.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**Q1.** In a gravity model of retail attraction, what happens to a store's pull as travel time increases, holding store size constant?
- (a) It increases
- (b) It decreases
- (c) It stays the same
- (d) It depends entirely on rent

**Q2.** O/X — In a typical neighborhood shopping center, the grocery anchor usually pays a *higher* base rent per square foot than the small inline shops beside it.

**Q3.** A retailer opens a second store four miles from its existing one and total company sales rise far less than the new store's own sales. What is this most likely called?
- (a) Co-tenancy
- (b) Percentage rent
- (c) Cannibalization
- (d) Daytime population

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Trade area** — the geographic zone a store draws its customers from, usually divided into primary, secondary, and tertiary rings.
- **Gravity model (Huff model)** — a method estimating the probability a shopper chooses a given store, where attraction rises with store size and falls with travel time.
- **Anchor tenant** — the large, traffic-generating store (often a supermarket or big box) that a shopping center is built around; it typically pays lower rent per square foot in exchange for the traffic it brings.
- **Co-tenancy clause** — a lease provision letting a small tenant reduce rent or exit if the anchor or a set share of the center goes vacant.
- **Cannibalization** — the share of a new store's sales taken from the retailer's own existing nearby locations rather than from competitors.

---

*Answers: **Q1 — (b).** In a gravity model, attraction is proportional to size and inversely related to distance or travel time raised to some exponent, so longer travel time means weaker pull. **Q2 — X (false).** The anchor generally pays the *lowest* rent per square foot in the center, because its role is to generate the traffic the inline tenants depend on; those small shops pay a premium for that spillover. **Q3 — (c) Cannibalization.** When trade areas overlap, part of the new store's revenue is transferred from an existing location rather than newly created — which is why site analysis models net incremental sales, not just gross sales at the new site.*
